title: GIAC GMON
summary: The GIAC Continuous Monitoring Certification, exam code GMON, is a defensive security certification from GIAC, the certification body of the SANS Institute. It is built for security operations centre analysts, incident responders and threat hunters who already work with logs and alerts. Passing it shows an employer that you can design detection, collect the right telemetry, spot suspicious activity in Linux and Windows hosts and in network traffic, and follow an incident through to a conclusion. The exam is proctored and combines multiple choice questions with performance based items, and GIAC exams allow a printed index that you prepare yourself. A pass is valid for several years and is renewed by earning continuing education credits. It leads to roles such as security operations analyst, detection engineer, threat hunter, incident responder or security monitoring lead. GIAC refreshes its exam outlines over time, so the domain list below follows the published outline and you should confirm the current version before booking. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: This is a certification from GIAC about watching a network and its computers for signs of attack. Continuous monitoring means collecting data all the time instead of only after a problem. The exam checks that you can find real attacks in that data and explain what you found. It is aimed at people who already work in a security team.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most organisations cannot review every alert by hand, so they need people who can build good detection. This certificate proves you understand both the data and the attacker behaviour behind it. It supports analyst, hunting and detection engineering roles, which are in steady demand. It also shows that you can write findings clearly, because reports matter as much as tools. For a defensive analyst, it is a strong signal of practical skill.
howItWorks: Learn what each log source records, such as system logs, web server logs and network flow records.
Set up a small practice lab with a monitoring platform and feed it sample data.
Study common attacker techniques and the traces each one leaves behind.
Practise writing detection rules and test them against known good and known bad traffic.
Build a topic index as you study, because you may bring a printed index into the exam.
Use the official practice test to get used to scenario and task based questions.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital where a reception computer suddenly starts connecting to a server it never touches. Nothing is broken, so nobody reports it. A monitoring analyst sees the unusual connection in the logs, links it to a login from a strange country, and raises an alert. Later the team finds the machine was infected the day before. The exam asks you to follow this kind of trail from a single strange event to a full picture, and to choose the right next step at each stage.
takeaways: Detection work depends on good data, so learn where logs come from and what they miss.
You need host knowledge as well as network knowledge, because attacks leave traces in both.
Start practising with a lab early, since tools only make sense once you feed them real data.

objectives: Explain the phases of continuous monitoring and how detection fits into security operations.
Identify the log and telemetry sources that reveal attacker activity.
Recognise common attack patterns on Linux and Windows hosts.
Build detection content and tune it to reduce false alarms.
Investigate an alert and document the findings clearly.
Support incident response with evidence collected from monitoring data.

chapters.title: Continuous monitoring and security operations foundations
objectives: Explain how a monitoring programme is organised and governed.
Describe the roles and workflows inside a security operations centre.
Select the log and telemetry sources that answer real detection questions.
Plan how alerts will be triaged, escalated and tracked to closure.
Measure whether a monitoring programme is actually working.

chapters.title: Designing and building monitoring architecture
objectives: Collect logs from hosts, applications and network devices reliably.
Normalise and enrich data so that searches return useful results.
Write correlation rules that combine several events into one alert.
Tune rules to cut false positives without losing real detections.
Protect the monitoring platform itself from tampering.

chapters.title: Linux host and application attack detection
objectives: Read system and service logs to spot unexpected process activity.
Detect persistence attempts such as altered start up scripts.
Recognise privilege escalation attempts on a Linux host.
Link web application attacks in access logs to activity on the server.
Explain what a rootkit or hidden process looks like in available evidence.

chapters.title: Windows host and application attack detection
objectives: Use Windows event logs to trace logon and process activity.
Detect credential theft techniques and the traces they leave.
Spot lateral movement between hosts in authentication records.
Identify suspicious scheduled tasks, services and registry changes.
Correlate endpoint alerts with network evidence during an investigation.

chapters.title: Network traffic and infrastructure monitoring
objectives: Analyse flow records to find unusual communication patterns.
Detect common network attacks such as scans, spoofing and tunnelling.
Investigate name resolution data for signs of malicious activity.
Identify connections to known bad destinations using threat intelligence.
Explain how encryption limits what network monitoring can reveal.

chapters.title: Incident handling and reporting
objectives: Follow a documented process from detection through containment and recovery.
Preserve evidence so that findings remain trustworthy.
Write a clear report for both technical and non technical readers.
Recommend changes that prevent a repeat of the same incident.
Brief decision makers during a live incident without overstating what is known.
